title: SaaS Website Launch Checklist: 12 Things to Test Before Going Live
summary: A practical pre-launch checklist covering tracking, accessibility, security, performance, customer support and search visibility.
content_html:
Launching a SaaS website involves much more than putting a landing page online. A reliable launch needs clear product messaging, secure account flows, accessible pages and a way to measure whether visitors can complete important tasks. This checklist helps teams catch costly problems before they reach real customers.

1. Explain your product in one sentence

Your opening section should identify the audience, the problem you solve and the main outcome. Avoid broad claims such as “revolutionary platform.” Ask someone unfamiliar with your business to explain the product after viewing the home page for ten seconds.

2. Test the entire signup journey

Create a new account using an email address that has never visited the site. Check validation messages, email confirmation, password reset and the first-run onboarding flow. Make sure a person can recover if they close the browser halfway through signup.

3. Check billing and plan information

Pricing should explain what is included, renewal intervals, trial conditions and cancellation rules. For paid subscriptions, verify that receipts, tax details and payment-failure messages are accurate. Use the payment provider's supported testing environment rather than real customer payments.

4. Set up meaningful analytics

Record a small set of events that answer business questions: signup started, signup completed, activation reached and upgrade completed. Do not track passwords or personal information in analytics event properties. Test consent settings and make sure reports do not double-count pageviews.

5. Prepare search-friendly page structure

Give each important page a unique title, helpful heading and descriptive URL. Include a crawlable explanation of what the product does. Use canonical URLs consistently, inspect the robots rules, and submit an accurate XML sitemap where supported. Avoid creating thin, nearly identical pages for every keyword variation.

6. Review mobile usability and accessibility

Navigate the site on a phone and with a keyboard. Ensure focus indicators are visible, forms have labels and error messages can be understood without color alone. Check buttons and menus at common screen sizes, especially when the on-screen keyboard is open.

7. Measure speed with realistic pages

Test your marketing landing page, signup page and dashboard separately. Pay attention to large images, unnecessary third-party scripts and layout shifts. Field data matters more than chasing a perfect laboratory score. Monitor real user experience as the audience grows.

8. Put basic security controls in place

Enforce HTTPS, use secure session cookies, restrict admin accounts and protect account endpoints against abuse. Make a documented plan for backups and incident response. Keep dependencies up to date and avoid putting secrets inside source repositories or frontend JavaScript.

9. Publish trust and support information

Make privacy, terms, contact information and support expectations easy to find. Clearly state what happens to customer data if they cancel. If you publish uptime or security claims, ensure they are factual and verifiable.

10. Validate important integrations

If users connect email, calendars, payment providers or other services, test both success and failure cases. A disconnected integration should produce a clear recovery path instead of silently losing information.

11. Build a rollback plan

Write down what to do if a deployment affects signup or payment. Confirm that database migrations can be handled safely, backups are restorable and team members know who can roll back a release.

12. Decide what success looks like after launch

Choose a baseline for activation, customer support requests, search traffic and conversion. Schedule a review of real user feedback, technical errors and search performance. Treat the first release as the start of learning, not the finish line.

Final check

Before opening the site to the public, ask a colleague to complete the primary customer journey without assistance. A short, realistic test often reveals problems that a long collection of feature screenshots cannot.
